It is settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755.

entities.text: R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;
(iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, discomfort,
disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."
15. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:

Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.

Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii), (a) and (iv).
It MACT No.276/2020

future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.

sentences.text: Medical Expenses:

17. Petitioner/injured (PW1) in his affidavit deposed that after the accident he was immediately taken to GTB Hospital where he was referred for surgery and admitted in the said hospital on 11.03.2020 and discharged after treatment.
PW1 deposed that thereafter he took treatment from different hospitals and he incurred expenditure of Rs.70,000/- on his medical treatment.
PW1 proved original medical bills Ex.PW1/2 (colly.).
Medical bill Ex.PW1/2 is single bill of Rs.145.60 paise.

18. Perusal of the medical record also shows that petitioner suffered fracture of right tibia and fibula, open grade III fracture of both bone, right leg fracture of bimalleur right leg and fracture of left leg, left great toe, traumatic amputation.
It also came on the record that petitioner suffered permanent disability to the extent of 68% in relation to both lower limbs (Ex.PW2/A).
In cross examination also PW1 denied the suggestion that he had not spent Rs.70,000/- for his medical treatment and stated that he is still taking the treatment of his accidental injuries.
Medical bill Ex.PW1/2 is only of Rs.145.60 paise.
Admittedly the entire treatment of the petitioner has been in GTB Hospital and Swami Dayanand Hospital, Dilshad Garden.

Except the bill Ex.PW1/2 there is no other document on the record, however considering the nature of the injuries this Tribunal finds on estimate basis that petitioner must have spent Rs.15,000/-
towards his medical expenses and accordingly same is awarded under the above said head.

Loss of earning during treatment:
19.

It has come on the record as well as in the evidence of PW1 that at the time of accident petitioner was working as a rickshaw puller and being self employed stated to be earning Rs.20,000/- per month.
There is although no documentary evidence of the earning of petitioner as rickshaw puller.
As such the notional income of the petitioner is taken at parity with minimum wages of unskilled worker in Delhi at the time of accident which is Rs.14,842/- per month.
20. Now coming to the period of treatment, this Tribunal has already noted above the different injuries suffered by the petitioner in the accident.
Medical treatment record is Ex.PW1/3 (colly.)
showing that petitioner remained hospitalized in GTB Hospital as well as in Swami Dayanand Hospital and continued taking treatment, petitioner suffered multiple fractures and amputation.
This Tribunal has already noted above that petitioner suffered permanent disability to the extent of 68% in relation to both lower limbs.
As such taking into consideration medical treatment record Ex.PW1/3, petitioner must have remained confined to bed and took treatment for period of nine months.
Therefore petitioner is entitled for loss of income for sum of Rs.1,33,578/- (Rs.14,842/- X 9 months).

sentences.text:
Relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:-
"9.
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so, the extent of such permanent disability.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).

The second step is to ascertain his MACT No.276/2020 Digitally signed by SHAILENDER Page 10 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.08 16:43:09 +0530 avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii)
Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

sentences.text: All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
(ii). The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the percentage of permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as percentage of permanent disability).

(iii). The doctor who treated an injured- claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.

Hon'ble Apex Court in the matter of Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar (supra) has laid down that Tribunal is bound to assess the evidence on the record, for the purpose of ascertaining the functional disability of the petitioner on account of medical permanent disability to assess how much the medical disability adversely affected on the functional capacity of the petitioner/injured so that just and fair amount of compensation can be ascertained under the heading of future loss of earning.
23. Keeping in view the ratio as discussed above, PW1 in his deposition stated that he was working as a goods rickshaw puller and was self employed at Delhi.
PW1 stated that the accident has totally curtailed his working capacity and due to serious injuries he is unable to handle his work by his own.

24.

Moreover one of the leg was amputated and medical board assessed the permanent disability of the petitioner to the extent of 68% in relation to both lower limbs.

NON PECUNIARY DAMAGES :
Pain & Sufferings:
30.

While discussing the criteria to ascertain the compensation for pain and sufferings by victim of vehicular accident, observations of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Satya Narain v. Jai Kishan, FAO No:
709/02, date of decision: 02.02.2007 can be considered:
"12. On account of pain and suffering, suffice would it be to note that it is difficult to measure pain and suffering in terms of a money value.
However, compensation which has to be paid must bear some objectives co-relation with the pain and suffering.

13. The objective facts relatable to pain and suffering would be:
(a) Nature of injury.
(b) Body part affected (c) Duration of the treatment."
31.

In this case, as per medical documents of the petitioner, he was found to have suffered fracture of right tibia and fabula, open grade III fracture both bone right leg, fracture of bimalleur right leg,
fracture of left leg and great toe traumatic amputation and other injuries.
His treatment record including medical disability certificate shows he sustained medical permanent disability to the extent of 68% in relation to both lower limbs.
It has also come on record that due to accidental injuries there was amputation.

Thus, it is clear that petitioner must have suffered pain and suffering during his treatment and therefore, this Tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of Rs.1,00,000/-
would be just and fair compensation for pain, sufferings and mental trauma suffered by the petitioner as MACT No.276/2020 SHAILENDER MALIK Page 15 MALIK Date: 2024.05.08 16:43:45 +0530 consequences of injuries sustained in the accident.
Accordingly, Rs.1,00,000/- is granted to the petitioner under this head.

Now, the question arises as to which of the respondent is liable to pay the compensation amount.
Insurance in its pleadings has taken the plea that it is not liable to make the payment of compensation as the offending vehicle was being plied, at the time of accident without any valid permit.

It is admitted position and came in DAR as well as in evidence of petitioner that at the time of accident the offending vehicle i.e. goods carrier Tata Motors no.DL-1GC-0623 was being used for transportation of water from the office of Delhi Jal Board.

37. Insurance company has examined one witness R3W1 examined on 05.12.2022 namely Mukesh Kumar Bharti from transport department, MLO Headquarter, Civil Line who has testified that he had brought the summoned record pertaining to above said vehicle no.DL-1GC-0623 which is Ex.R3W1/B, Ex.R3W1/C and Ex.R3W1/D.

sentences.text: Since the witness though was examined on behalf of insurance but did not support the case/claim of the insurance company, same witness was summoned again by insurance company who was again examined on 14.09.2023.

This time this witness simply stated that there is no document on the record of MLO Headquarter regarding vehicle no.DL-1GC-0623 to show that it was exempted from keeping any permit as stated by him earlier.
39. Thus the same witness made two contradictory statements at different point of time.

In cross examination recorded on 14.09.2023, witness stated that he was given a document i.e.
communication dated MACT No.276/2020 by SHAILENDER Page 17 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.08 16:44:05 +0530 21.03.2016 by his MLO which is Mark PX, on the basis of which he had earlier stated that said vehicle does not require any permit as was being used by Delhi Jal Board for water supply.

40. Perusal of that document Mark PX shows that it is a communication from State Transport Authority to Delhi Jal Board, communicating that any vehicle being used in Delhi Jal Board, in terms of Section 66 of M.V. Act, would not be required to have permit when it is being used as transport vehicle for State/Government.
It is evident from the facts that the tanker was being used for supply of water by Delhi Jal Board, there is no dispute to that fact.

In such situation when a particular evidence has already been recorded regarding such vehicle do not require any permit on account of document Mark PX, on which this Tribunal can take judicial notice, therefore subsequent evidence given by the same witness (R3W1) would be of no consequence in view of his cross examination also.

41. Another witness examined on behalf of insurance is R3W1 Ms.Pooja, Administrative Officer who stated that she has brought the record regarding notice served under Order XII Rule 8 CPC through lawyer of the insurance company to owner and driver of vehicle no.DL-1GC-0623 which is Ex.R3W1/1 and postal receipts, returned envelope are Ex.R3W1/2 to Ex.R3W1/4 and report of investigator is Ex.R3W1/5.
42.

Having considered such evidence of R3W1, such evidence can also be of no consequence for respondent no.3 to get exemption from liability to pay the compensation, firstly because even if there is a notice under Order XII Rule 8 CPC but postal receipts and returned envelopes do not establish that same was ever served to respondent no.1 and 2 herein.

Returned envelopes rather mention the endorsement that no person by the MACT No.276/2020 Digitally signed by SHAILENDER Page 18 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.08 16:44:12 +0530 name of respondent no.1 and 2 reside at the given address.

In such circumstance when respondent no.1 and 2 have never apepared in the witness box, mere exhibition of notice under Order XII Rule 8 CPC,
postal receipts etc. does not establish that owner and driver were ever served and despite being served they failed to file the original documents as called for.
Similarly report of investigator Ex.R3W1/5 can be of no help when investigator himself has not been examined.
It established law that mere exhibition of a document is no proof of said document.

No doubt in inquiry proceedings of accident claim Tribunal, strict proof is not required but atleast there must be some cogent evidence establishing a fact because mere assertion of any fact in itself is not sufficient.
Thus for the reasons stated above this Tribunal concludes that insurance company is liable to pay the compensation.

Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so, the extent of such permanent disability.
This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
(i) Whether the disablement is permanent or temporary;
(ii) If the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement;
(iii) If the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.
After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.
The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii)
Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
As such the notional income of the petitioner is taken at parity with minimum wages of unskilled worker in Delhi at the time of accident which is Rs.14,842/- per month.
As such taking into consideration medical treatment record Ex.PW1/3, petitioner must have remained confined to bed and took treatment for period of nine months.
Therefore petitioner is entitled for loss of income for sum of Rs.1,33,578/- (Rs.14,842/- X 9 months).
All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
